name: Hosting Chevron documentation with GitHub Pages and Doxygen
summary:
**Conversation Overview**

The person is working on a C++ library called Chevron and sought validation and guidance on a documentation strategy they had conceived. Their core idea was to use Doxygen to generate HTML documentation and publish it to a GitHub repository hosted via GitHub Pages, creating a publicly accessible documentation website. They wanted to confirm that GitHub Pages works as they understood it, that the Doxygen-to-GitHub-Pages pipeline is technically sound and practical, and that the update workflow (modifying source comments, regenerating HTML, pushing to the documentation repository) is viable. They also expressed interest in customizing the Doxygen output beyond vanilla defaults to make the documentation feel more specific to the Chevron project, while acknowledging that a minimal viable product with default styling was acceptable as a starting point.

Claude confirmed the approach is sound and well-established in the C++ open source ecosystem, noting that libraries like nlohmann/json, fmt, spdlog, and Catch2 use essentially the same pipeline. Claude introduced an alternative structural option — using a `gh-pages` branch within the Chevron repository itself rather than a dedicated documentation repository — and explained the tradeoffs between the two approaches. Claude also noted the need for a `.nojekyll` file to prevent GitHub Pages from running Jekyll on the Doxygen output. On the customization front, Claude explained the key Doxyfile configuration levers (`HTML_EXTRA_STYLESHEET`, `HTML_HEADER`, `HTML_FOOTER`, `HTML_STYLESHEET`, `LAYOUT_FILE`, `PROJECT_LOGO`, `USE_MDFILE_AS_MAINPAGE`) and specifically recommended the `jothepro/doxygen-awesome-css` repository as a drop-in stylesheet that modernizes Doxygen's appearance with minimal effort. Claude also recommended setting up GitHub Actions early to automate the regeneration and deployment step on every push to main.

chat_messages.text: So it is my understanding that GitHub has this feature with repositories that allows you to host a free website under a GitHub URL, do I have that correct? If so, I had this idea that I wanted to run by you and see what you thought of it. I was trying to identify some practical ways to present beautiful documentation for Chevron publicly to users so that they can understand how the library works or if they need a reference for whatever reason. And I realized that I have been sitting on top of the possible answer all along. I think I should have realized before considering that it is essentially what Doxygen is for, but I can use Doxygen to generate the HTML documentation and publish it to a dedicated repository to host the documentation online publicly. The practical part about this is that when documentation changes in the code, the generated docs are updated and those updates can then be pushed directly to the Chevron documentation repository to update the live website. Is this idea I have sound? Is this really a possible approach to tackling this issue? One of the other things I was thinking about was getting deeper into the customization of the Doxyfile to make the webpages more "Chevron" than default vanilla Doxygen. I don't mind the vanilla Doxygen to start just to get a "minimal viable product" if you will, but I do want to better understand how I can customize what is generated by Doxygen so that we can control what the documentation looks like. If we could make this happen we would be in a really great spot. There would be not too much work involved with updating documentation (merely changing comments in source/header files and regenerating the HTML) aside from the initial workload of customizing the webpages beyond the defaults Doxygen has in place. But of course, none of this matters if anything I said here was incorrect and I've got it all wrong. I need you to let me know how sane this idea is and if I can really pull it off. Most importantly, is it really practical? I would like to hear your thoughts on the matter.

The user is asking about using GitHub Pages to host documentation and whether Doxygen is a good fit for generating and publishing C++ library docs to that platform. They want to understand the practical workflow and customization options for making the documentation look polished.

GitHub Pages is indeed free static hosting with URLs like `username.github.io` or `username.github.io/repo-name`, and it can serve Doxygen's HTML output directly—you'd just add a `.nojekyll` file to prevent Jekyll from processing the files. This is actually a very common pattern in the C++ community; projects like nlohmann/json, fmt, Catch2, and spdlog all use this exact approach. The typical workflow involves generating the docs locally with Doxygen and pushing them to either a `gh-pages` branch or a `/docs` folder on the main branch, and GitHub automatically serves them from there.

The user's idea of a separate documentation repository is perfectly valid—it keeps the main repo clean and avoids bloating the history with generated files—but the more conventional approach is using a `gh-pages` branch in the same repository, which is simpler to maintain and easier to automate with GitHub Actions. Either way works, though the dedicated repo does add some sync overhead between repositories.

For actually customizing Doxygen to look better, there are several practical options: the Doxyfile has tons of built-in configuration for layout and content filtering, you can layer on custom CSS through the stylesheet options, or you can use a third-party theme like Doxygen Awesome CSS which gives it a modern look with minimal effort. There's also the option to generate and edit a layout file to restructure the navigation, or point to a markdown file as the main landing page.

Beyond just styling, you can add logos and branding through the navbar, and if Graphviz is installed, Doxygen can automatically generate class and inheritance diagrams. While there are alternative documentation stacks like Sphinx with Breathe or MkDocs, for a C++ project like Chevron, vanilla Doxygen paired with Doxygen Awesome CSS is probably the most practical sweet spot.

The user's approach is solid—it's exactly how most C++ open source projects handle documentation. The workflow of updating comments, regenerating, and pushing is standard, and CI/CD can easily automate the regeneration step. I'm confident about GitHub Pages and Doxygen as established technologies, though I could verify the specific URL for Doxygen Awesome CSS to be thorough. The idea is sound and practical—it's one of the most well-established documentation pipelines in C++ open source. GitHub Pages is exactly what you described: free static hosting tied to a repository, serving at `username.github.io/repository-name` by default. It works seamlessly with Doxygen output since it's just static HTML/CSS/JS.

There are actually two structural approaches worth considering. You can use a dedicated documentation repository as you're proposing, or keep the generated docs in a separate branch (usually `gh-pages`) within the Chevron repo itself. Both are common and functional, though the branch approach has some practical tradeoffs I should walk through.

The branch method is more conventional and avoids maintaining a second repository, but a dedicated repo keeps your main history clean of generated content and is equally legitimate. Either choice works fine—it mostly comes down to how you want to organize your CI pipeline.

The update flow you're describing is exactly how this works in practice: modify Doxygen comments, regenerate the HTML, push the output. The key is automating that last step early with GitHub Actions, which can run Doxygen on every push to main and deploy automatically. Once that's set up, the documentation becomes a pure function of your source tree and you never touch it manually again.

For customization, vanilla Doxygen looks dated because the default stylesheet hasn't held up well, not because of any fundamental limitation. You've got several levers to pull: you can add custom CSS that layers on top of the defaults without replacing them entirely, or you can take full control of the page structure by replacing the header, footer, and stylesheet. There's also an XML layout file you can generate and modify to reorganize the sidebar and navigation order.

For branding, you can set the project logo, name, and brief description in the navbar. If you want a custom landing page, point Doxygen at a Markdown file instead of letting it generate an index.

The real game-changer here is Doxygen Awesome CSS — it's a ready-made stylesheet that makes vanilla Doxygen look genuinely modern with dark mode, better typography, and a light/dark toggle. You just point the extra stylesheet setting at it and you're done.

So the minimal viable product is straightforward: use vanilla Doxygen with Doxygen Awesome CSS, set your Markdown file as the main page, add a logo, and set up a GitHub Actions workflow to rebuild and deploy on every push. That gets you a professional-looking documentation site in hours instead of weeks, and you can refine the styling and navigation later.

This approach isn't novel at all — nlohmann/json, fmt, spdlog, Catch2, and basically every modern C++ library does exactly this. You're following an established pattern that's proven to work well.

GitHub Pages is exactly what you described: a free static site hosting service tied to a repository. Sites are served at `username.github.io/repository-name` by default (or just `username.github.io` if the repository is named that way). It serves arbitrary static HTML/CSS/JS, which makes it a natural fit for Doxygen output. The one small wrinkle is that GitHub Pages runs Jekyll by default on the served content; for Doxygen output you drop a `.nojekyll` file at the root to bypass that, which is a one-line operation.

One thing worth knowing up front: you have two reasonable structural choices, not just one. You can do what you're proposing — a dedicated documentation repository — or you can use a separate branch (conventionally `gh-pages`) inside the Chevron repo itself. Both work and both are common. The branch approach has a slight edge in being more conventional and avoiding the overhead of a second repo, but a dedicated repo keeps the main repo's history free of generated artifacts and is perfectly legitimate. The choice is mostly about taste and how you want to organize your CI.

The update flow you described is exactly how this works in practice: change Doxygen comments, regenerate, push. The "push" step is the one worth automating early — GitHub Actions can run Doxygen on every push to main and deploy the result automatically. Once that's wired up, you genuinely never touch the docs manually again. The doc site becomes a pure function of the source tree, which is the property you actually want.

Now the customization question, which is the more interesting half.

Vanilla Doxygen looks dated because the default stylesheet has aged poorly, not because Doxygen itself is limited. The relevant knobs:

- `HTML_EXTRA_STYLESHEET` — supply additional CSS that layers over the defaults without replacing them. Lightest-touch path.
- `HTML_HEADER`, `HTML_FOOTER`, `HTML_STYLESHEET` — full replacement of the page chrome. More work, more control.
- `LAYOUT_FILE` — generate with `doxygen -l`, then edit. Controls page structure and sidebar navigation order; useful for reorganizing, hiding sections, or inserting custom pages.
- `PROJECT_LOGO`, `PROJECT_NAME`, `PROJECT_BRIEF` — navbar branding.
- `USE_MDFILE_AS_MAINPAGE` — point Doxygen at a Markdown file (your `Chevron.md`, for instance) and it becomes the landing page rather than a generated index.

The most useful pointer I can give you: look at **Doxygen Awesome CSS** (the `jothepro/doxygen-awesome-css` repository on GitHub). It's a drop-in stylesheet that transforms vanilla Doxygen into something that genuinely looks modern — clean typography, sensible spacing, light/dark toggle, the works. You point `HTML_EXTRA_STYLESHEET` at its CSS files and you're done. A lot of serious C++ libraries use it as their starting point precisely because it gets you from "embarrassing default" to "looks intentional" in minutes rather than days. From there you can layer your own overrides for color palette, fonts, and accents to make it specifically Chevron without rebuilding the whole stylesheet from scratch.

So the practical MVP recipe is: vanilla Doxygen + Doxygen Awesome CSS, mainpage pointed at a Markdown landing page, your logo in the navbar, a `.nojekyll` file at the root, and a GitHub Actions workflow that regenerates and deploys on every push to main. That gets you to a respectable public documentation site with hours of work rather than weeks. The deeper customization — custom layout, full chrome replacement, bespoke landing pages — is something you layer in over time once the pipeline itself is solid.

One last note: nothing about this is unusual or experimental. nlohmann/json, fmt, spdlog, Catch2, and most modern C++ libraries publish their docs essentially this way. You're not blazing a trail — you're stepping onto a well-paved one, which is exactly what you want for infrastructure work that isn't itself the point of the project.
